text:
Statement against arbitrary content takedown and account restrictions faced by public representatives and journalists

Earlier today, @Meta restricted the Instagram accounts (“Platform”) of @AamAadmiParty (AAP), its national convener @ArvindKejriwal, and Mohammed Zubair (@zoo_bear), co-founder of @AltNews. 

Over the past week, along with these instances, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has also recorded several instances of content takedowns faced by media organisations including @PeekTV_in, cartoonists such as @cartoonistrrs and @cartoonistvish, and @SauravDassss - @Cockroachisback's spokesperson.

According to the publicly available information, the affected posts were restricted pursuant to the “legal requests” received by the Platform. In many cases, users are provided little or no meaningful explanation about the legal or factual basis of the restriction or what steps they can take to challenge the decision. Such opaque moderation practices undermine users’ ability to understand how platform policies are enforced and make it difficult to distinguish between legitimate moderation and arbitrary or inconsistent decision-making. This is especially concerning where the affected content relates to political expression, criticism of public authorities, or peaceful protest, all of which occupy a central place in democratic discourse.

The Supreme Court of India upheld the constitutionality of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (“IT Act”), on the basis that the statutory framework required that blocking orders be reasoned, necessary, and proportionate, and that such reasons must be recorded in writing to enable judicial review. By contrast, in most of these cases, notices sent to social media intermediaries through the Sahyog Portal under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act and Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, leave users in the dark, with no recourse to meaningfully challenge takedowns and leave affected parties without legal redressal. The Sahyog Portal puts in place a parallel system to take down content online, without any of the safeguards present under Section 69A.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has consistently advocated against these practices. We are concerned that this takedown drive is contrary to the rule of law and to India’s constitutional commitment to freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.

While private platforms are not directly bound by the Constitution in the same manner as the State, their content moderation decisions increasingly influence the digital spaces in which democratic participation takes place. This places a heightened responsibility on platforms to ensure that their moderation processes are transparent, consistently applied, and accompanied by adequate procedural safeguards, including notice, reasons for enforcement actions, and effective mechanisms for review. At the same time, any direction issued by public authorities requiring platforms to restrict lawful online speech must comply with constitutional safeguards and the legal procedures prescribed under Indian law. Informal or opaque restrictions on political speech or press freedom undermine public trust and democratic accountability.

In light of the above, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls for the following:

- Immediate disclosure of all takedown orders issued to platforms, including specific reasons and legal justifications.

- Strict adherence to the procedural safeguards laid out under Section 69A and the 2009 Blocking Rules, under the IT Act, which were upheld by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India.

- Notices received by social media intermediaries to be sent to every user affected to ensure transparency.

- Strengthening of independent oversight and appellate mechanisms to ensure that users can effectively challenge unlawful restrictions.

- Greater transparency from platforms regarding the number, nature, source, and outcome of governmental requests/orders for content removal and account restriction.

Statement on the Indian government's order to GitHub to block BitChat:

The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (@Cyberdost ) under the Ministry of Home Affairs (@PIBHomeAffairs) has ordered GitHub (@github) to remove three URLs linking to BitChat, an app that works offline without an internet connection and enables users to communicate over Bluetooth. This order was issued under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021.

During the internet shutdowns imposed on multiple occasions over the past week in parts of Central Delhi, many protesters faced difficulties communicating or seeking emergency services. Open-source applications like BitChat allow people to communicate with other people using the same application nearby, without an internet connection.

The order states that the application would impede the state's ability to conduct lawful interception and surveillance and enable users to circumvent lawful restrictions such as internet shutdowns. The notice was issued at 11:16 PM on 23rd July and has given GitHub three hours to remove the links.

However, the order fails to satisfy the tests of legality, necessity, and proportionality and constitutes as an abject misuse of Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules 2021.

At the outset, Section 79(3)(b) does not confer the power to block or remove content, which instead stems from Section 69A of the IT Act. The issuance of orders with generic grounds is further inconsistent with the safeguards laid down by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Supreme Court upheld Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 strictly because it required that blocking orders must be reasoned, necessary, and proportionate, and that such reasons must be recorded in writing to enable judicial review.

The opacity surrounding these removals goes against the strict requirements of accountability and record-keeping embedded in the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009.

The only reason this particular order in the current instance became public is not due to dissemination by the issuing authority, but rather because @Jack posted about the same on X. What we see emerging through these removals is a system of informal, decentralised censorship, where the government can direct content removals without transparency or oversight.

The lack of information renders a meaningful legal challenge impossible and leaves affected parties without legal redressal, including the basic elements of review that Section 69A provides when read with the Blocking Rules 2009. Orders passed under Section 79(3)(b) therefore function as circumventions of the procedural safeguards enumerated under Section 69A of the IT Act.

#FOSS #internetshutdown

text:
Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

text:
https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s statement on the Delhi Police notice directing X to remove content from the platform.

According to media reports, the Intelligence Fusion and Strategic Operations (“IFSO”) unit of the Delhi Police Special Cell has issued several notices to X, citing the IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 (“IT Rules 2021”), following complaints filed with the Delhi Police alleging circulation of “derogatory, malicious and defamatory content” targeting constitutional heads, particularly the Prime Minister, on the social media platform. The IFSO has also registered an F.I.R. under Sections 351(3), 353(2) and 356(2) of the Bharatiya Nyay Sanhita 2023, against several social media handles for posting such content.

In its “Intimation to Intermediary for Disabling Access to Unlawful Information” notices issued to X,  purportedly under provisions of IT Rules 2021, the IFSO directed the platform to:

- Delete/remove the alleged post/video from the platform immediately.

- Provide the complete registrant details including full name, address, contact details and email ID, of the X account ID holder who posted such content, as well as the login and logout details of the said account, along with corresponding time and date stamp, or any other details relevant for investigation.

 - To preserve information/ records relating to the said posts for future investigation, and furnish a certificate u/s  63(4) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, in respect thereof.

This is not the first instance of large-scale removal of posts, as even earlier on 27 July 2026, Delhi Police reportedly instructed multiple social media intermediaries to take down posts/videos uploaded during the Jantar Mantar Protests that allegedly contained offensive or abusive remarks against the Prime Minister. Moreover, the Delhi Police’s social media monitoring team has been specifically engaged in monitoring online platforms for such content, and upon identifying objectionable posts, notices are issued to the concerned intermediaries directing them to remove the identified content.

At the outset, the legislative scheme of the IT Act 2000, does not contemplate/ permit the authorisation of the Delhi Police to direct the takedown of online content from social media platforms.

The power to block public access to online information or content is exclusively traceable to Section 69A of the IT Act 2000, which vests such power solely in the Central Government, or an officer specially authorised by it.  Whereas, Section 79(3)(b) of IT Act merely grants safe harbour to intermediaries, subject to compliance with due diligence obligations. In no circumstance can Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act 2000 or IT Rules 2021 confer a power upon the Central or State Government to devise a mechanism or appoint any agency/ officer for regulating or restricting free speech online. Reliance is placed on Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1 (para 121).

Notably, the IT (Blocking) Rules 2009 already outline procedure and rules for the designation of an officer, not below the rank of Joint Secretary, empowered to issue directions under Section 69A for blocking public access to online information. However, neither Section 69A nor the IT (Blocking) Rules, 2009 authorise the Central Government, or any State executive, to constitute a Nodal Agency empowered to direct the blocking of public access to online content.

Despite the above legislative scheme, on 26 December 2024, the Lieutenant Governor of the NCT of Delhi, purportedly in exercise of powers under the first proviso to Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT  Rules 2021 read with Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act 2000, issued a Notification appointing the Delhi Police as the Nodal Agency and Deputy Commissioners of Police (of various divisions) as designated officers for issuing takedown notices. Consequently, the Delhi Police has been issuing takedown notices pursuant to the said Notification.  However, this Notification, being founded upon a provision and subordinate legislation that do not authorise the creation of such a mechanism, is ex facie illegal and ultra vires the IT Act 2000. The legality of the said Notification has been challenged by https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 in a Petition before the Delhi High Court on the aforesaid ground, among others. The Petition is registered as W.P.(C) 7650/2025, titled “Software Freedom Law Center, India v. State of NCT of Delhi & Ors.”

Without prejudice to the aforesaid, both Section 69A and Section 79(3)(b) read with IT Rules 2021, outline overbroad grounds. While Section 69A empowers the Central Government to issue notice for blocking public access to online information on overbroad grounds such as "public order"; Section 79(3)(b) read with the IT Rules 2021 outline expansive grounds such as content’s use in the commission of an unlawful act relating to public order, decency or morality, defamation, etc., or where such information is prohibited under any prevailing law.  Since these grounds are decided by an executive order, without any judicial determination, their overbroad nature renders them susceptible to misuse and overreach. Therefore, even mere profanity, satire, or genuine criticism may be directed to be removed pursuant to such orders. This leaves the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression vulnerable.

The risk of misuse and overreach is further exacerbated by the compliance regime applicable to intermediaries. An intermediary is likely to err on the side of over-compliance rather than independently assess the legality of a removal request, owing to the extremely limited timeline for compliance and the severe consequences of non-compliance. Under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules 2021, an intermediary is required to comply with a removal order within three hours, leaving virtually no scope for any meaningful independent assessment to guard against misuse or excessive application of such powers. Further, failure to comply exposes the intermediary to the risk of imprisonment for up to 7 years and fine for requests issued u.s. 69 A [Section 69A(3)], or the loss of safe harbour protection for orders issued u.s. 79(3)(b) [Section 79].

Moreover, when mere profanity expressed in anger against a governmental policy, or as part of political criticism, becomes the subject of penal investigation, it seriously undermines the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression. We condemn any penal action in such circumstances, as it creates a significant chilling effect on the exercise of free speech by citizens, who are entitled to express their disagreement, dissatisfaction, or anger towards governmental policies through peaceful expression and dialogue.

To safeguard the online freedom of speech of these users, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s RightsLine provides free legal assistance and support to anyone facing content takedowns or account suspensions. Our team can help individuals understand their options and navigate the available redress mechanisms. 

Report at https://t.co/jzMiSxaaBB or mail us at rightsline@sflc.in

Statement on MeitY's notice to WhatsApp over the "usernames" feature

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has sent WhatsApp a notice about the usernames feature it announced on 29 June 2026. The notice asks the company to explain, within three days, why regulatory action should not be taken against it "for launching a feature that may increase cybercrimes", and it directs the company "not to roll out this feature until the consultation on this point is achieved to the satisfaction of the Government". The Internet Freedom Foundation is concerned that the notice has no clear basis in law. It is an attempt by the executive to decide what a company may build and ship, which no statute permits.

The notice treats the launch of a lawful feature as a wrong the company must justify. That reverses the ordinary position especially given the absence of any clear legal power that exists. MeitY does not name any provision that lets it approve a product feature before release or order one withdrawn, because there is none, and the provisions it does cite do not supply that power.

Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 is a safe harbour that protects an intermediary from liability for what its users post, so long as it observes due diligence. It decides when a platform can be held liable. It is not a power for MeitY to decide what features the platform may offer. Sections 66C and 66D punish identity theft and cheating by personation. They are criminal offences, tried by courts, aimed at the person who steals an identity, not at the maker of a tool that a third party misuses. Also, on MeitY's logic, a telecom operator could be told not to sell SIM cards because SIM cards are used in almost every online fraud. 

Rule 3(1)(b), Rule 3(2) and Rule 4 of the IT Rules, 2021 are due diligence and grievance obligations and cannot be converted into a licensing scheme. Section 69A, the one provision that lets MeitY control what appears online, permits the blocking of specific information through a set procedure. It says nothing about which features a company may build. Further the IT Rules, 2021 are subordinate legislation made under Sections 79 and 87 of the IT Act, and subordinate rules cannot travel beyond the parent statute (Ajoy Kumar Banerjee v. Union of India). If a rule cannot exceed the Act, a letter certainly cannot. The power to require prior permission for a feature is not in the Act, not in the Rules, and cannot be created by a notice. 

MeitY has tried this before. In March 2024 it told the same large intermediaries, among them AI Companies, to obtain its explicit permission before deploying under-tested AI models. That was criticised as an overreach that sought to build a licensing mechanism with no empowering provision in the IT Act, and within a fortnight MeitY withdrew it and dropped the permission requirement. This notice repeats the move for a single feature and goes further, because it names one company, sets a three-day clock, and bars the launch until MeitY is satisfied. 

This matters beyond WhatsApp. A power asserted against one company by letter can be turned on any company and any feature. On this reasoning MeitY could tell a browser not to switch on a privacy setting by default, or a payments app not to add a login method, each time until it was content. The notice also invokes traceability, through Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 and the identification of the "first originator" of a message. Rule 4(2) has been challenged as exceeding its parent provision and resting on no law made by Parliament, and that challenge is pending before the Delhi High Court. Raising it against a feature meant to share fewer identifiers fits a pattern. 

We ask MeitY to state the exact provision of law under which this notice, and the direction to halt the roll-out, has been issued, and to withdraw that direction. It should stop using Section 79 and the contested traceability rule as leverage to control product design and to reverse features that improve privacy. Impersonation and fraud are real risks, but they are met by enforcing the criminal law against those who commit them, and by open processes that rest on identified legal powers. They are not met by MeitY deciding, in private and by letter, what features Indians may use. That is a licence raj for software features.

New Delhi, 1 July 2026

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

I’ll match the column’s categories—maps, election challenges, domestic force, and institutional pressure—with what Democrats have actually https://t.co/jbADowdQwD the same categories the column treats as coup preparation, Democrats have used the same tools when they held the levers. The differences are mostly of degree, timing, and which party’s media called it normal. **Redistricting.** Illinois Democrats, after the 2020 census, drew a congressional map designed to leave Republicans with 3 of 17 seats, the party’s weakest share there since the Civil War. Courts left it in place. Maryland Democrats have repeatedly redrawn the 6th District to flip a longtime Republican seat; a state judge in 2022 called one version an extreme partisan gerrymander drawn with “near surgical precision,” then Democrats still controlled the replacement. New York’s Democratic legislature bypassed its commission and passed maps struck down in *Harkenrider v. Hochul* (2022); later maps still targeted Republican seats. In 2025 California voters passed Proposition 50, suspending the independent commission through 2030 so the legislature could draw a map projected to add up to five Democratic House seats. That is the mirror image of the Texas mid-decade redraw the column treats as authoritarian. Both parties do it where they can; independent commissions are the exception, not the rule. **Refusing results.** House Democrats objected to counting electoral votes after every recent Republican presidential win: Florida in 2001 (Alcee Hastings, Maxine Waters, and others, citing “deliberate fraud” and suppression; no senator joined, so Al Gore gaveled them down), Ohio in 2005 (Stephanie Tubbs Jones and Barbara Boxer forced separate House and Senate debates; both chambers rejected the objection), and several states in 2017 (House members only; Joe Biden gaveled them down). Hillary Clinton later called Trump’s win illegitimate and said the election was stolen; dozens of Democrats skipped the inauguration on that basis. Stacey Abrams never conceded the 2018 Georgia governor’s race and described it as stolen. Those efforts did not include a Capitol riot or 147 House members plus eight senators objecting, which is the real scale difference in 2021. The precedent of treating a loss as illegitimate was already established. **National Guard and domestic force.** In 2020, governors in more than 30 states—including Democrats such as Minnesota’s Tim Walz—activated roughly 32,000 to 43,000 National Guard troops during the George Floyd protests, for curfews, property protection, and crowd control. In Washington, more than 5,000 Guard members from D.C. and other states were on the streets around the White House; active-duty units were staged nearby. That was under a Republican president, but Democratic mayors and governors requested or accepted Guard deployments in their own cities (Minneapolis, and earlier Ferguson and Baltimore under Democratic local leadership). The legal theory—Guard under state or Title 32 status to back law enforcement during unrest—is the same one now disputed when Trump federalizes Guard units for immigration or crime operations. Posse Comitatus limits active-duty troops; it has not stopped either party from using the Guard when the politics fit. **Institutional pressure.** Democratic administrations have also fired or sidelined officials, steered grants and contracts, leaned on universities and nonprofits through funding conditions, and used the Justice Department against political opponents (the Trump cases brought by state and federal Democratic prosecutors are the obvious recent example; earlier ones include IRS scrutiny of conservative groups under Obama). Emergency powers were stretched for COVID: extended mail voting, business closures, and eviction moratoria that courts later trimmed. None of that is a secret plan to seize ballot boxes. It is the ordinary use of federal and state power by the party that holds it, described as defending democracy when Democrats do it and as a coup when Republicans do it. The column’s last step—an intention to federalize the Guard, seize ballot boxes, and declare winners—has no matching Democratic operation on the record either. What both parties do in a close cycle is redraw maps, litigate results, question the other side’s procedures, and talk about emergencies. The coup language is what changes with the speaker, not the underlying conduct.

Bad becomes worse? Further changes proposed to the proposed changes to IT Rules!

Today, post-noon on 21 April 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has published further proposed amendments to the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Second Amendment Rules, 2026.

The notice states that these are limited to Rule 3(3)(a)(ii) requiring that labels identifying synthetically generated information be continuously and clearly visible throughout the duration of the content in visual display. This goes beyond the earlier requirement of “prominent” visibility, and now mandates persistent, uninterrupted disclosure for the entire duration of such content. This requirement is applicable to all users of social media and AI tools, and not just digital news platforms.

All other provisions in the newly updated draft remain the same as the draft circulated on 30 March 2026. Our comments to the MeitY are available here. The consultation timeline has now been extended allowing stakeholders to submit comments on both the earlier draft amendments and these additional amendments by 07 May 2026. We note that suggesting changes within the window of a pre-existing public consultation process in which thousands of Indians have voiced opposition is likely to result in, “consultation fatigue” and at the very least demonstrates a pattern of ad-hoc policy making than one which accounts for structured and planned feedback.

Further, MeitY has once again indicated that the submissions will be held in fiduciary capacity in MeitY and shall not be disclosed to any one at any stage, enabling persons to submit feedback/comments freely without any hesitation. Importantly, consultation processes are important for democratic decision making, placing the responses in the public domain would ensure meaningful engagement and participation by stakeholders. It would also allow for better analysis, understanding, and fair critique of the various perspectives put forward. We therefore urge MeitY to place the comments and feedback on their website in the interest of democracy and transparency.

We urge citizenry to participate in such public consultation and share their feedback/comments on the draft rules in a rule wise manner by email to itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in in MS Word or PDF format by 07th May, 2026. We have drafted a short template email which readers can improvise upon.

As of today, more than 4500 people have used our link to improve upon and send their own comments to MeitY primarily asking for a withdrawal of the proposed changes to the IT Rules, 2021.

🛜 🌍 The world's biggest domain seller GoDaddy says India's fight against fake websites could make the internet less safe. A fight not many are watching,  but is set to reshape internet governance, we report at @Reuters 

🌍Let's understand the background -- India has a fake-website problem. For years, fraudsters have registered domains impersonating global brands -- bogus Amazon shopping sites, fake McDonald's franchise offers, phony Microsoft support pages -- to con ordinary people. Dozens of companies took them to court.

🌍 What happened in December 2025? a Delhi judge cracked down. She blocked more than 1,100 fraudulent sites. But she didn't stop there.

She wrote sweeping new rules for the entire domain industry: strip away privacy protection by default, hand over website owners' details within 72 hours to anyone claiming a "legitimate interest," and block any web address resembling a protected brand.

🌍 The big news now: Now GoDaddy -- which runs 80 million domains worldwide -- is fighting back in thousands of pages of court filings my colleagues and I reviewed . Its warning is striking: the rules would make the internet less safe, not more. They'd expose ordinary website owners to stalking and harassment. And because domain systems are global, an order from one Delhi courtroom could ripple across the entire web -- potentially forcing GoDaddy to "exit India" altogether.

🌍 They are colourful filings: One of GoDaddy's arguments? That you can't ban the word "McDonald" -- it's a Scottish surname meaning "son of the world ruler."  The U.S. giant also submitted research compiled from the Merriam-Webster's website to argue that safeguarding variations of a protected trademark like "HUL" - Unilever's Indian unit, could overlap with 118 English words that contain the string, like "hulk" and "moghul".

🌍 It's a landmark collision between a nation trying to protect its citizens and the borderless architecture of the internet itself.

Two members of Congress have been quietly merging two separate site-blocking bills into one.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

1.95 lakh blocking orders were given by @narendramodi govt in just five months on social media

Between March and July 2026, govt directions involving Instagram, Facebook and YouTube reportedly surged to around 1,275 a day — one every 68 seconds. the number of URLs referred for blocking was reportedly nearly 2.98 lakh.

Has the Indian internet become a place where criticism can be removed faster than citizens can publish it?

When technology can connect govt requests directly into platform systems, the real issue isn't just how many posts disappear.

It is how much scrutiny, transparency & accountability exists before they disappear.

A democracy should not fear questions.
A govt should not fear criticism.
And citizens should never have to wonder whether speaking up will make their voice vanish with a click.

The internet gave ordinary Indians a voice. A govt which believes in Digital India must ensure that voice is protected — not progressively squeezed by the delete button.

How to access Polymarket in India without a VPN.

Indian ISPs (Jio, Airtel, Vi, BSNL) have blocked @Polymarket at the DNS level.

Steps to fix it ⬇️

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
ANDROID

1. Settings → Network & Internet (or Connections)
2. Tap Private DNS
3. Select "Private DNS provider hostname"
4. Enter: https://t.co/vGTkSv7Un9
5. Save

Alternative hostname: https://t.co/uozbWpgpS7

Works on both Wi-Fi AND mobile data. Encrypted by default. Easiest method of all.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
iPHONE / iPAD

Wi-Fi only (iOS limitation):
1. Settings → Wi-Fi → tap (i) next to your network
2. Configure DNS → Manual
3. Remove existing entries
4. Add 1.1.1.1 and 1.0.0.1
5. Save

For mobile data: install the "1.1.1.1: Faster Internet" app by Cloudflare from App Store. It sets up a system-wide profile.

The app uses iOS's VPN framework but is NOT a real VPN. It doesn't hide your IP or change location. It just reroutes DNS queries system-wide. Free, no signup, made by Cloudflare.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
WINDOWS 11 / 10

1. Settings → Network & Internet → Wi-Fi (or Ethernet)
2. Click your active connection
3. Scroll to "DNS server assignment" → Edit
4. Change to Manual → toggle IPv4 on
5. Preferred: 1.1.1.1 | Alternate: 1.0.0.1
6. Save

Press Windows key → type "cmd" → right-click "Command Prompt" → Run as administrator → Yes. Black window opens. Type ipconfig /flushdns, press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
macOS

1. System Settings → Network
2. Click your active connection → Details
3. Click DNS in sidebar
4. Click + and add 1.1.1.1, then 1.0.0.1
5. Remove existing ISP entries (select, click −)
6. OK → Apply

Open Terminal: press Cmd + Space → type "Terminal" → Enter. Copy-paste sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder, press Enter, type your Mac password (invisible while typing, that's normal), press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
ROUTER (covers every device on Wi-Fi)

1. Open 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1 in browser
2. Login (credentials usually on router sticker)
3. Find DNS settings (under WAN, Internet, or DHCP)
4. Primary: 1.1.1.1 | Secondary: 1.0.0.1
5. Save and reboot router

Best option if you want laptop + phone + smart TV + everything to work without per-device setup.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
VERIFY IT WORKED

Open browser: visit https://1.1.1.1/help

It'll confirm you're using Cloudflare DNS + whether DNS-over-HTTPS is active. Then try polymarket(dot)com

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
IF DNS ALONE DOESN'T WORK

Some ISPs use Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) or SNI-based blocking. In that case:

• Use Firefox or Brave → enable DNS-over-HTTPS in settings (encrypts the DNS query so ISP can't see it)

• Android Private DNS method above already does this by default

Two members of Congress have been quietly merging two separate site-blocking bills into one.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

Legal framework for Internet Shutdown in India

Context: During the "Chalo Sansad" protest organised by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), Mobile Internet Service were shut down in parts of Central Delhi.

Provisions:

~Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunication Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, Telecommunication services may be suspended.

~Suspension can be ordered only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing.

~Orders must be reasoned, published, geographically and temporarily limited and consider whether less restrictive measures are sufficient.

Under the 2024 Rules, a suspension order cannot remain in force for more than 15 days.

Supreme Court Guidelines:

~In Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India (2020), the Supreme Court linked Internet access with freedoms under Articles 19(1) (a) and 19(1)(g).

~Shutdowns must satisfy necessity and proportionality, be the least restrictive measures, and remain open to judicial review.

Suspension can be challenged in court?
Yes. Under Article 226 before a High Court and Article 32 before the Supreme Court.

India's Position:
India recorded about 24 Internet shutdowns in 2026 till July 22; Jammu & Kashmir has recorded the highest cumulative number since 2012.

text:
🚨 Exposing a brand in India? 

Before you post, you need to know if they can actually get your video taken down for speaking your truth."

[Do Not Skip This Part]👇
Note: This tweet is only for general understanding of how this happens. A recent tracking down of a video involving the brand has occurred. Here is a thread to understand how it happens. Please refrain from mentioning the brand name or creator name in comments or replies to this tweet. 
 
In India, there is no simple rule allowing a brand to remove a video simply because it criticizes the brand. 

The usual route is a mix of:

IT Act + IT Rules + platform policy + civil court injunction/defamation/commercial disparagement suit.

1) What is the core legal structure?

Platforms like YouTube, X, Instagram, etc. are treated as intermediaries. They get “safe harbor” protection for user-generated content, but they may lose that protection if they ignore valid legal directions.

Under India’s intermediary framework, a platform gets legally strong “actual knowledge” mainly through:

A court order, or
A government/authorized agency direction/intimation

A private brand complaint alone usually does not automatically force a platform to remove a video. 

The Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India - clarified that platforms should not be forced to decide legality merely based on private complaints; the stronger trigger is a court order or government direction.

2) How does a brand complaint become a court order?

The structure usually works like this:

Step 1: The brand's legal team collects evidence

The company gathers the video URL, transcript, screenshots, claims made in the video, alleged false statements, impact on reputation, possible business loss, and proof of harm.

Step 2: The brand's legal team may send a legal notice

This is often the first pressure step. The brand may demand a takedown, an apology, a correction, damages, or the removal of specific claims.

Step 3: The brand files a civil/commercial suit.

If the creator does not comply, the brand can file a case for defamation, commercial disparagement, trademark issues, unfair trade practice, or reputational/business harm.

Step 4: The brand asks for urgent interim relief

The brand may request an interim injunction, sometimes ex parte, meaning the court can issue a temporary order without first hearing the creator if it believes urgent harm may occur.

Step 5: The court checks the matter prima facie

At this stage, the court is not finally deciding who is right. It checks whether there is an arguable case that the content may be false, misleading, malicious, defamatory, or commercially disparaging.

Step 6: The court may pass an injunction

The order can direct the creator to remove the video, stop sharing it, stop repeating certain claims, or restrain publication of similar allegedly disparaging content.

Step 7: The court order is sent to the platform
Once YouTube/X/Instagram receives the order, the platform may remove or disable access to the video to comply and protect its intermediary safe harbor.

3) Does the brand need to contact the platform grievance officer?

They can, but for defamation or brand-disparagement disputes, the platform may not want to act purely on the brand’s private complaint unless the violation is very clear under platform policy.

The more powerful route is:

Brand → Court → Court order → Platform compliance

The grievance officer becomes important when the platform receives a complaint, legal notice, or court/government order. But the grievance officer is not usually the final judge of whether a review is defamatory or fair criticism.

4) Can a video be removed just because it criticizes a company?

No. Criticism alone should not be enough.

A creator can usually criticize a product, company, service, pricing, quality, privacy policy, design, marketing claims, or consumer experience.

But risk increases when the video makes strong factual claims, such as:

“this phone is fake”
“this company is cheating customers”
“this is just a rebranded phone”
“do not buy this because the company is lying”
“this brand is a scam”

These claims need proof. If the creator presents them as facts and the company says they are false, misleading, malicious, or damaging to business, the company may go to court.

5) What does the court usually look at?

For a temporary injunction, the court may consider:

Prima facie case: Is there an arguable case that the content is false, misleading, defamatory, or commercially disparaging?

Balance of convenience: Who will suffer more harm if the order is or is not granted?

Irreparable harm: Can the damage to reputation or business be fixed later with money, or is immediate restraint needed?

Proof and testing: Did the creator rely on reliable documents, technical tests, expert analysis, official sources, or only assumptions?

Language used: Was the tone fair and analytical, or aggressive and conclusive without enough proof?

6) What can the creator do after an ex parte order?

The creator can challenge the order in the same court. 

They can ask the court to vacate or modify the injunction and argue that:
the video was fair comment,
the claims were based on evidence,
the company suppressed facts,
the order was passed without hearing the creator,
the takedown is too broad,
or public interest requires the video to remain available.

7) Practical creator lesson

A review video is safer when it clearly separates:

Opinion: “In my view, this looks like poor value.”

Fact: “The model number matches X device.”

Evidence: screenshots, teardown, software logs, official filings, import data, product pages, privacy policy, benchmark/test method.

Limitations: “Based on my testing,” “I could not independently verify X,” “the brand has been contacted for comment.”

The danger zone is when the creator makes a strong factual allegation without showing a reliable testing method or source.

Important point:
Fair criticism is not illegal. But factual claims like “fake phone”, “rebranded phone”, “scam”, “company is cheating” need strong proof.

Disclaimer: I have shared only how the law is applied in such cases; this tweet does not reflect my opinion or view on any similar incident. 

Bookmark this for the future; this will be useful for a lot of creators out there.

In Shaurya Alloys Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Punjab & Another & connected matters, CWP-34296-2024, pronounced on 01.10.2026, the Punjab & Haryana High Court has laid down an important framework for application of Section 16(2)(c) of the CGST Act.

✅ Validity of Section 16(2)(c) read with Section 155 upheld, but the provision cannot be used in isolation to automatically reverse ITC merely because the supplier failed to pay tax. The officer must examine the genuineness of the transaction and surrounding circumstances.

🚫 Supplier cancellation, nil/short tax payment or departmental alerts are only triggers for inquiry — they are not, by themselves, sufficient grounds for ITC denial.

🔍 Before proceeding against the buyer, the Department must examine the supplier, invoices, relevant tax period, nature of default and recovery action already taken against the supplier.

📑 Where fraud is alleged under Section 74/74A, the SCN itself must contain facts connecting the purchaser with such fraud; supplier-side fraud cannot simply be transferred to the recipient.

🧾 Though the purchaser bears the burden under Section 155, eligibility may be established through invoices, e-way bills, transport documents, weighbridge slips, stock/consumption records and proof of actual receipt of supplies.

💰 Double recovery is impermissible. Tax already recovered from/deposited by the supplier must be considered, along with permissible re-availment of ITC; importantly, the law applicable to the relevant tax period must be applied.

👂 Taxpayers are entitled to personal hearing and a reasoned speaking order; where third-party statements are relied upon, a request for cross-examination must be considered by a reasoned order.

🛑 For the pending batch, taxpayers at SCN stage were allowed 8 weeks to file supplementary replies/evidence, and the Court directed that no fresh coercive recovery action be taken until fresh decisions are passed.

📌 Key Takeaway: Section 16(2)(c) remains valid, but ITC cannot be reversed mechanically. Supplier default must be examined through proper investigation, taxpayer evidence and due process before liability is fastened on the purchaser.
